reconcile.connective: Clarke harmonizes the Gospels by positing two or three separate cups — offered before and during the crucifixion — so each evangelist describes a different moment.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells's Skeptic's Annotated Bible lists all four differing accounts of the drink side by side under one heading, without attempting to reconcile them.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.work: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible ("What did the soldiers give Jesus to drink?", skepticsannotatedbible.com/contra/vinegar.html)
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "What did the soldiers give Jesus to drink?"

excerpts.excerpt_text: It appears that at least two cups were given to our Lord; one before he was nailed to the cross, viz. of wine mingled with myrrh, and another of vinegar, while he hung on the cross. Some think there were three cups: One of wine mixed with myrrh; the Second, of vinegar mingled with gall; and the Third, of simple vinegar. Allow these three cups, and the different expressions in all the evangelists will be included.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly harmonizes all three drink-descriptions (Matt 27:34 vinegar+gall, Mark 15:23 wine+myrrh, and the later plain-vinegar offers in Mark 15:36/Luke 23:36/John 19:29) by positing two or three separate cups offered at different moments, so each evangelist reports a different offer rather than a conflicting one. NOT shipped.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874), p. 325, "Christ's last drink of one kind. Of a different kind."
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats this passage directly under that heading, arguing from a comparison of Matt 27:34 and 27:48 that drink was offered to Jesus twice — a drugged cup he refused, then an undrugged one he accepted — and that the word rendered 'gall' denotes any intense bitterness, including myrrh.
